# James Cutting — Shot Lengths & the Rhythm of Attention in Hollywood Film

**Source work:** Cutting, DeLong & Nothelfer (2010), "Attention and the Evolution of Hollywood Film", *Psychological Science* 21(3), 432–439 (+ Cutting's wider cinemetrics programme)
**Evidence tag: 🟢 for the measurements; 🟡 for the "use this rhythm" rule**

**Sources opened (in the harvest):**
- Original paper record + abstract, APA PsycNET: Cutting, DeLong & Nothelfer (2010), "Attention and the Evolution of Hollywood Film", *Psychological Science* 21(3), 432–439.
- The full paper PDF (author-side copy, jordandelong.com).
- Smith & Christie dialogue — contains Tim Smith's summary of Cutting's ASL numbers.
- Wikipedia biography page (programme-level summary: 300+ films, 1915–2015; 2018 follow-up study).

## (a) Core finding
Popular Hollywood films have steadily evolved toward the natural rhythm of human
attention. Shot lengths did not just get shorter — the *sequence* of shot lengths in
modern films increasingly follows a 1/f ("pink noise") pattern, the same fluctuation
pattern found in human reaction times and attention. In plain words: neighbouring shots
tend to have similar lengths, with slow waves of longer/shorter shots nested inside each
other, instead of random or metronome-regular lengths. Cutting's wider programme also
found modern films have more motion, shorter scenes, fewer dissolves, more close-ups,
less clutter and higher contrast than older films — every change pushes in the direction
of holding the viewer's attention.

## (b) Evidence base
Large-scale quantitative corpus analysis ("cinemetrics"): the 2010 paper parsed **150
films (1935–2005)** shot by shot (231 shots in *The Seven Year Itch*, 1950, up to 3,099
in *King Kong*, 2005; mean ≈ 1,132 shots per film). Tim Smith's published summary of the
programme gives the headline number: average shot length fell from **≈15 seconds to
≈3.5 seconds** across 160 Hollywood films, 1935–2010 (Smith citing Cutting et al., 2011 —
the 2011 paper itself was not opened in the harvest run; the figure is as reported by Smith).
A 2018 follow-up found filmmakers had also adapted motion, sound amplitude and scene
durations to match natural attention fluctuations (per Wikipedia summary of the study).
This is peer-reviewed, repeatedly extended corpus measurement — about as solid as film
research gets. Honest limit: the data prove films *did* evolve this way; the claim that a
1/f rhythm *causes* better attention-holding is the authors' theory-linked interpretation,
not a controlled retention experiment.

## (c) Tag: 🟢 for the measurements; 🟡 for the "use this rhythm" rule
Reason: the shot-length and 1/f findings are peer-reviewed and replicated across a
300+ film programme (🟢), but the step from "hit films look like this" to "your video
will retain better if you copy it" is an inference, not a measured A/B result (🟡).

## (d) Editing rules it converts into
- **R-CUT-1 (ASL band):** IF the video is a fast-paced popular-format video, THEN keep
  average shot length in the modern band (≈3–6 s); long stretches well above this read as
  "slow/old" to a modern audience. 🟡
- **R-CUT-2 (no metronome):** IF consecutive shots have near-identical lengths for a long
  run, THEN vary them — neighbouring shots should resemble each other, but the sequence
  must breathe in waves (clusters of short shots inside stretches of longer ones, 1/f-like),
  never a fixed beat. 🟡
- **R-CUT-3 (climax compression):** IF the sequence approaches its climax/payoff, THEN
  progressively shorten shots and increase motion; after the payoff, lengthen shots again
  to let it land. (Pattern from Cutting's "evolution of pace" abstract — seen in search
  results only, paper not opened in full: treat as 🟡/UNVERIFIED-in-full.)
- **R-CUT-4 (declutter):** IF a frame has competing subjects/clutter, THEN prefer the
  closer, cleaner framing — the century-long trend is toward fewer elements per frame,
  which is attention control, not fashion. 🟡
